summary: FireSignal is a spatiotemporal machine learning model that produces a next day fire activity risk score across a 100 km grid of Australia. I harmonised 486,255 NASA MODIS and VIIRS detections into a historical grid and trained an XGBoost model on it. A same cell persistence baseline scores AUC 0.807 and my base model scores 0.810. Adding a feature for previous day neighbouring fire activity lifts AUC to 0.854, so neighbouring cell information adds +0.047 beyond persistence. The model retains useful skill on unseen data (0.843 trained on 2019 and tested on 2020; 0.790 median across geographic holdouts). Most of the predictive skill is persistence, and I report that openly, along with the failure to predict fire severity (CV R² -0.11). FireSignal is a regional triage layer to help agencies decide where to look first, and probability calibration is the next step before operational use.
details:
The Problem & The Impact
In the 2019–2020 Black Summer, 33 people lost their lives, 17 to 24 million hectares burned, more than 3,000 houses were destroyed, and an estimated 3 billion animals were killed or displaced. I built FireSignal to ask a practical question: can harmonised satellite data help fire agencies decide where to look first, so resources can be pre-positioned sooner?

What it does (and what it predicts)
FireSignal produces a relative risk score for satellite detected fire activity in each 100 km grid cell over the following 24 hours. A positive event is any thermal anomaly detected by NASA FIRMS in that cell the next day. It is a regional triage layer, not a dispatch tool. The scores are not yet calibrated probabilities.

How it works
I harmonised 486,255 NASA MODIS and VIIRS fire detections into 249,246 daily grid records across 681 cells. I trained an XGBoost model on weather, drought (KBDI), population density, and human infrastructure data. I then added a feature that asks "was there a fire in neighbouring cells yesterday?" Neighbouring cell activity added predictive signal beyond persistence, lifting AUC from 0.810 to 0.854.

Validation results
All figures are AUC unless stated, where 0.5 is chance.

  • Same-cell persistence baseline: 0.807
  • Base model (weather, drought, infrastructure): 0.810
  • Spatial model: 0.854
  • +0.047 over persistence
  • +0.044 over the base model (paired bootstrap, 2,000 iterations, 95% CI +0.041 to +0.047, p < 0.001)
  • Forward in time (train 2019, test 2020): 0.843
  • Median geographic holdout (trained on one region, tested on another): 0.790
  • Cells with no fire the previous day: 0.697. This excludes same-cell persistence, but a fire spreading in from a neighbouring cell can still count.
  • PR-AUC: 0.543 on an imbalanced dataset
  • Severity prediction (cross-validated R²): -0.11. The model failed to predict fire size.

Most of the model's skill comes from persistence. Weather, drought, and infrastructure add little over persistence at this resolution (0.810 versus 0.807). Neighbouring-cell information adds a further +0.047.

Fire behaviour and the 98% statistic
In 1,021 cause-attributed fires from the Mulgar dataset (Monash University), 98% of the fires in the highest detection-count category were lightning-associated. That category is the top 10% of fires by satellite detections (229 or more detections within 11 km over 7 days), which included 103 fires. This points to the challenge of monitoring remote fires. It is not a claim about all Australian bushfires. Human-associated fires sat nearer roads (about 232 m) and fire stations (about 6.5 km) than remote, lightning-associated fires (about 958 m and 14.2 km).

Limitations

  • The 100 km grid shows where to look, not where to send a crew.
  • Scores are uncalibrated. Isotonic calibration is the next step before operational use.
  • The model was trained on 2019–20 and demonstrated on NSW, so other seasons and states are untested.
  • Severity (fire size) was not predictable from this data.
  • The tool hasn't been tested with any fire agency.

Tools and Languages
Python, Google Colab, XGBoost, scikit-learn, SHAP (explainable AI), Streamlit, and PyDeck. I used Qwen3 (8B), run locally via Ollama, for data cleaning scripts, coordinate debugging, and Streamlit code. Claude (Anthropic) helped with the presentation deck's design and layout. Methodology, model selection, validation, and results are my own.
